report_title: Agrius / Agonizing Serpens (G1030) Actor Intelligence Pack — Stage-1 CTI Extraction
source: MITRE ATT&CK G1030 (https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1030/); SentinelLabs 'From Wiper to Ransomware | The Evolution of Agrius', Amitai Ben Shushan Ehrlich, 2021-05-25 (https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/from-wiper-to-ransomware-the-evolution-of-agrius/); Palo Alto Unit 42 'Agonizing Serpens (Aka Agrius) Targeting the Israeli Higher Education and Tech Sectors', 2023-11 (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/agonizing-serpens-targets-israeli-tech-higher-ed-sectors/). Additional corroboration referenced by the above: ESET WeLiveSecurity 'Fantasy — a new Agrius wiper deployed through a supply-chain attack'; Check Point 'Agrius Deploys Moneybird'. This actor has NO local seed; the TTP set is built from G1030 (22 group-level techniques) enriched with Impact/defense-evasion tradecraft from the two named vendor reports.

actor.name: Agrius
actor.attribution: Iran-nexus destructive actor active since 2020, notable for destructive wiper and fake-ransomware operations concentrated on Israeli targets. Public reporting (Microsoft) has linked Agrius to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), per MITRE ATT&CK G1030. Multiple vendors (SentinelLabs, Unit 42, Check Point, ESET) independently track the cluster and its destructive tooling. Nexus (Iranian state-aligned, MOIS-linked) is asserted rather than a single named unit; the wiper-masquerading-as-ransomware pattern is a signature behavior.

key_campaigns.name: Initial wiper campaign (Apostle / DEADWOOD masquerading as ransomware)
key_campaigns.summary: After initial espionage activity, Agrius deployed destructive wiper attacks against Israeli targets, masquerading the destruction as ransomware. Attacks used DEADWOOD (aka Detbosit), the novel Apostle wiper, and the custom .NET IPsec Helper backdoor. Apostle was later rewritten into functional ransomware. Initial access via exploitation of public-facing apps (incl. CVE-2018-13379 in FortiOS) and ASPXSpy web shells for RDP tunneling and lateral movement.

key_campaigns.name: BlackShadow operations against Israeli targets
key_campaigns.summary: Destructive and extortion-flavored operations (data theft plus wiping) attributed to the same Agrius/BlackShadow cluster targeting Israeli organizations, continuing the theft-then-destroy pattern.

key_campaigns.name: Agonizing Serpens — Israeli higher-education and tech sector attacks
key_campaigns.summary: Data-theft-then-destruction campaign against Israeli higher-education and technology organizations. The group stole PII and IP using a custom database extractor (Sqlextractor / sql.net4.exe), then deployed three novel wipers — MultiLayer, PartialWasher, and BFG Agonizer — to cover tracks and render endpoints unusable. Used ASPXSpy-variant web shells (Uploader.aspx, xcopy.aspx, css.aspx), Mimikatz, SMB brute/spray, GMER and Rentdrv2 vulnerable drivers to disable security tooling, and PuTTY/pscp for exfiltration.

malware: ASPXSpy web shell (variants: Uploader.aspx, xcopy.aspx, css.aspx)

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius typically uses commercial VPN services such as ProtonVPN to anonymize last-hop traffic into victim networks.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — off-victim infrastructure acquisition is not observable in defender host/network logs; hunt candidate via inbound-connection geo/ASN anomaly analytics (commercial-VPN egress hitting exposed apps/RDP)

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius exploits internet-facing applications for initial access, including widespread attempts to exploit CVE-2018-13379 in Fortinet FortiOS SSL-VPN and SQL-injection activity against web applications.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — exploitation of known CVEs and SQLi is detectable via WAF/IDS signatures, vulnerable-appliance version telemetry, and anomalous post-auth VPN sessions, but n-day exploitation of edge devices often precedes visibility

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius acquires valid domain credentials through brute force, spraying and dumping, then reuses them for follow-on lateral movement and RDP access via compromised accounts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — authentication with legitimate credentials blends with normal activity; hunt candidate via impossible-travel, off-hours logon, and RDP-from-web-shell-host correlation

ttps.procedure_description: Following exploitation, Agrius deploys variants of the ASPXSpy web shell (observed filenames Uploader.aspx, xcopy.aspx, css.aspx) on internet-facing servers to maintain access and proxy follow-on commands.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — new .aspx files in web-root paths and w3wp.exe/IIS worker spawning cmd.exe are strong, well-covered detection signals

ttps.technique_name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
ttps.procedure_description: Agrius deployed the IPsec Helper .NET backdoor post-exploitation and registered it as a Windows service for persistence.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — new service creation (Event ID 7045 / registry Services key writes) pointing at unusual binaries is highly detectable

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
ttps.procedure_description: Agrius uses ASPXSpy web shells to enable follow-on command execution via cmd.exe on compromised servers.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — cmd.exe spawned by an IIS worker (w3wp.exe) or other web-server parent is a classic web-shell command-execution detection

ttps.procedure_description: The MultiLayer wiper uses a DeleteLogs() function to create a scheduled task that launches a batch script once, which then removes all Windows Event Logs before self-cleanup.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — scheduled-task creation (Event ID 4698 / Task Scheduler operational) launching a one-time batch that clears logs is a strong, anomalous signal

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius deployed base64-encoded variants of the ASPXSpy web shell that decode at runtime to evade static detection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — base64-heavy .aspx content and runtime decode routines are detectable via web-content inspection and script-block/AMSI telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
ttps.procedure_description: Agrius used several mechanisms to disable security tooling: modifying EDR-related services to prevent auto-start on reboot, and abusing vulnerable signed drivers — GMER64.sys/gmer64.sys (renamed AGMT.sys, via loader agmt.exe) and Rentdrv2 (via loader drvIX.exe) — to selectively stop and remove security-software processes (BYOVD).
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — vulnerable-driver loads (Microsoft vulnerable-driver blocklist / Sysmon driver-load) and EDR-service tampering are detectable, but BYOVD kernel action can blind the very sensor meant to see it

ttps.technique_name: Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs
ttps.procedure_description: The MultiLayer wiper clears all Windows Event Logs via a scheduled batch script as an anti-forensic step during its destructive routine.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — event-log clearing (Security 1102 / System 104) is a discrete, high-fidelity signal, ideally forwarded off-host before the wipe completes

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius masqueraded tooling by renaming binaries — e.g. the Plink tunneling tool renamed to systems.exe, and the GMER driver renamed AGMT.sys — to blend with legitimate system files.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — renamed-binary masquerading evades name-based rules; hunt candidate via original-filename (PE VERSIONINFO) vs on-disk-name mismatch and known-tool hash matching

ttps.procedure_description: The MultiLayer wiper removes all files it uses (dropped assembly, batch scripts, itself) after execution to remain stealthy and hinder forensics.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — self-deletion of just-created executables is detectable via file-create-then-delete sequences in EDR, but overlaps with benign cleanup

ttps.procedure_description: The MultiLayer wiper timestomps files by overwriting LastAccessTime, LastWriteTime and CreationTime — setting NTFS timestamps to 1601-01-01 and non-NTFS to 1980-01-01 — a well-known anti-forensic technique.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — timestamp manipulation leaves minimal live telemetry; hunt candidate via MFT $STANDARD_INFORMATION vs $FILE_NAME timestamp divergence in forensic triage

ttps.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Embedded Payloads
ttps.procedure_description: Agrius wipers (e.g. MultiLayer) carry embedded payloads — a dropped assembly file and batch scripts — that are written out and executed at runtime, then deleted.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — embedded payloads are opaque until extraction; hunt candidate via static/entropy analysis of the sample rather than host log detection

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius used Mimikatz (filename Mimi.exe) and ProcDump to dump LSASS memory and capture credentials in victim environments.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — LSASS process access with dump rights (Sysmon EID 10 / EDR credential-theft analytics) and ProcDump against lsass are high-fidelity detections

ttps.technique_name: OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager
ttps.procedure_description: Agrius dumped the SAM database on victim machines to capture local account credentials.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — SAM/registry-hive access and reg save of HKLM\SAM are detectable via registry-access and process-command-line telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius engaged in brute-forcing activity via SMB within victim environments to obtain valid credentials.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — bursts of SMB/NTLM logon failures (Event ID 4625) from a single internal host are readily detectable

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius performed password spraying via SMB against many accounts in victim environments.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — many accounts each seeing a single failed SMB logon from one source is a classic spray signature (4625 fan-out)

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius used open-source port scanners — WinEggDrop and NimScan — to perform detailed scans of hosts of interest inside victim networks.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — internal horizontal port-scanning generates detectable connection fan-out and unusual scanner-binary execution, though scan tooling is easily renamed

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius used the NBTscan tool to enumerate remote, accessible hosts in victim environments.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — NetBIOS name-scan bursts across a subnet and NBTscan execution are detectable, but blend with legitimate admin discovery

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius tunnels RDP traffic through deployed web shells and via the Plink tool to access victim environments with compromised accounts and move laterally.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — RDP tunneled over web shell / Plink shows as anomalous localhost-relayed RDP and RDP sourced from a web-server host; detectable via lateral-RDP and tunnel analytics

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius downloaded follow-on payloads for execution from legitimate file-sharing services such as ufile.io and easyupload.io, and moved tooling between hosts inside victim networks.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — internal SMB tool copies and downloads from consumer file-sharing sites are detectable via proxy category and internal file-write telemetry, but ride trusted transfer channels

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius gathered data from database and other critical servers in victim environments prior to using wiping mechanisms as an anti-analysis/anti-forensics step.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — reading local files/DB content is high-volume normal activity; hunt candidate via bulk-access-then-stage-then-wipe sequencing correlation

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius used a custom tool, Sqlextractor (binary sql.net4.exe), to query SQL databases and automatically identify and extract PII (ID numbers, passport scans, emails, addresses), saving results to CSV files.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — a non-application process issuing bulk SQL SELECT queries against DB servers and writing large CSVs is detectable via DB audit logs and endpoint file-create telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius staged data for exfiltration in a local working folder, C:\windows\temp\s\, before archiving and transfer.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — accumulation of archive/CSV/.dmp files in C:\windows\temp\s\ is a detectable staging pattern via file-path monitoring

ttps.technique_name: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility
ttps.procedure_description: Agrius used 7zip to archive extracted data (producing .7z / .ezip files) in preparation for exfiltration.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — 7zip/archive utility spawning against staged data directories is detectable via process-command-line telemetry, though archiving is common admin activity

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius exfiltrated staged data using tools such as PuTTY, pscp.exe and WinSCP, connecting outbound to command-and-control servers over SSH/SCP.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — pscp/WinSCP outbound SSH to external hosts from a server, transferring .7z/.ezip/.dmp files, is detectable via egress SSH monitoring and process-network correlation

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius's defining behavior: after data theft, it deploys wipers (Apostle, DEADWOOD/Detbosit, Fantasy, MultiLayer, PartialWasher, BFG Agonizer) to destroy data on victim endpoints and servers, rendering them unusable and covering the actors' tracks — often masqueraded as ransomware.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — mass file overwrite/deletion produces a detectable burst of file-modification and I/O; detection value is early containment, since by wipe time impact is occurring. Prioritize pre-wipe precursors (BYOVD, log clearing, VSS deletion)

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius masqueraded destructive operations as ransomware, dropping ransom notes as a ruse; the Apostle wiper was later rewritten into fully functional ransomware, and the Moneybird ransomware was deployed in later Israeli-targeted attacks. In many incidents the 'ransomware' was cover for irrecoverable wiping.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — high-rate file encryption with extension changes and ransom-note drops is detectable via file-entropy/canary and note-creation analytics, but the fake-ransomware ruse means recovery may be impossible regardless

ttps.procedure_description: The MultiLayer wiper deletes all Volume Shadow Copies and then removes the Volume Shadow Copy (VSS) service itself to prevent data restoration before destroying the disk.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — shadow-copy deletion (vssadmin/wmic/WMI) and VSS service removal are high-fidelity ransomware/wiper precursors and among the most reliable early-warning detections

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius wipers destroy on-disk content — e.g. BFG Agonizer offers modes to write ~420 MB of binary data to a target device to make a drive unusable and to wipe files in specified folders; MultiLayer and PartialWasher similarly overwrite/destroy file and drive content.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — large sequential raw writes to physical drives / mass overwrite of file content is detectable via disk-I/O and raw-device-handle telemetry, but is concurrent with the impact itself

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius wipers corrupt disk structures to prevent boot: BFG Agonizer opens a handle to \\.\PhysicalDrive0, detects MBR/GPT partition style, and overwrites the first 6 sectors (boot sector); MultiLayer opens \\.\PhysicalDrive0 and wipes the first 512 bytes so the system can no longer boot.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — a user-mode process obtaining a raw \\.\PhysicalDrive handle and writing to the boot sector/MBR is a rare, high-fidelity destructive signal (EDR raw-disk-write analytics)

ttps.procedure_description: Agrius stops and removes services to enable destruction and disable defenses — abusing GMER/Rentdrv2 drivers to stop and remove security-software processes/services, and removing the Volume Shadow Copy (VSS) service during the MultiLayer wipe.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — abnormal stopping/removal of security and VSS services (service-state change events) is detectable, though driver-level process termination may bypass service-control logging

ttps.procedure_description: After corrupting disk structures, Agrius wipers ensure the victim system can no longer boot and trigger shutdown/reboot to finalize the destructive impact, leaving endpoints inoperable.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — a shutdown/reboot call is trivially common and only meaningful as the terminal step of a wipe chain; hunt candidate via correlation with preceding raw-disk-write/log-clear events

detection_signals: New or modified .aspx file in an IIS web root (Uploader.aspx / xcopy.aspx / css.aspx or base64-heavy ASPXSpy content) followed by w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe
RDP session sourced from an internet-facing web server, or RDP relayed through Plink/localhost tunnel — web-shell-tunneled lateral movement
Vulnerable-driver load of gmer64.sys / AGMT.sys or Rentdrv2 (agmt.exe / drvIX.exe loaders) — BYOVD to kill security tooling (Microsoft vulnerable-driver blocklist / Sysmon EID 6)
EDR/AV service configuration changed to disable auto-start on reboot, or security services stopped/removed shortly before mass file activity
Volume Shadow Copy deletion AND removal of the VSS service (vssadmin/wmic/WMI) — high-fidelity wiper/ransomware precursor
User-mode process opening a raw \\.\PhysicalDrive0 handle and writing to the boot sector / first sectors (MBR/GPT) — disk-structure wipe (MultiLayer / BFG Agonizer)
Scheduled task created to run a one-time batch that clears all Windows Event Logs (4698 followed by 1102/104) — MultiLayer DeleteLogs()
Mimikatz (Mimi.exe) or ProcDump accessing lsass.exe, or reg save of HKLM\SAM — credential dumping
SMB logon-failure fan-out from one internal host (4625) across many accounts — password spraying/brute force
sql.net4.exe (Sqlextractor) or a non-application process issuing bulk SQL queries and writing large CSV files, then 7zip archiving to C:\windows\temp\s\
pscp.exe / WinSCP outbound SSH from a server transferring .7z / .ezip / .dmp files — exfiltration over C2
Internal file-create-then-self-delete of a just-dropped executable plus timestomping to 1601-01-01 / 1980-01-01 — wiper anti-forensics
notes: TTP set built from MITRE ATT&CK G1030 (22 group-level techniques, all retained: T1583, T1560.001, T1119, T1110, T1110.003, T1059.003, T1543.003, T1005, T1074.001, T1140, T1685, T1041, T1190, T1570, T1036, T1046, T1003.001, T1003.002, T1021.001, T1018, T1505.003, T1078.002) and enriched with Impact and defense-evasion tradecraft sourced directly from the two named vendor reports. 12 techniques added beyond the G1030 group set, each vendor-cited: T1053.005, T1685.005, T1070.004, T1070.006, T1027.009, T1485, T1486, T1490, T1561.001, T1561.002, T1489, T1529. Total 34 techniques. FRAMEWORK-VERSION NOTE: in this ATT&CK build, 'Disable or Modify Tools' is the current top-level technique T1685 (tactic defense-impairment) with sub-technique T1685.005 'Clear Windows Event Logs'; the legacy T1562.001 is REVOKED. IDs are emitted per the current authoritative dataset (verified via get_technique). IMPACT TACTIC (7 techniques — the library's first destructive actor, well represented): T1485 Data Destruction, T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact (wiper-as-ransomware ruse + Apostle-to-ransomware + Moneybird), T1490 Inhibit System Recovery (VSS deletion + VSS service removal), T1561.001 Disk Content Wipe, T1561.002 Disk Structure Wipe (BFG boot-sector / MultiLayer PhysicalDrive0 first-512-byte overwrite), T1489 Service Stop, T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot. The wipers named — Apostle, DEADWOOD/Detbosit, Fantasy, MultiLayer, PartialWasher, BFG Agonizer — show code overlap (shared codebase / same developers) per Unit 42. LOW detection-feasibility techniques (route to HUNTING, not signature detection): T1583 (off-victim VPN infra), T1078.002 (valid-account reuse), T1036 (renamed-binary masquerading — Plink->systems.exe, GMER->AGMT.sys), T1070.006 (timestomp — forensic-triage only), T1027.009 (embedded payloads — sample analysis), T1005 (bulk local read), T1529 (shutdown only meaningful in wipe-chain correlation). HIGHEST-VALUE EARLY-WARNING detections (route to DETECTION): T1490 (shadow-copy + VSS-service deletion), T1561.002 (raw \\.\PhysicalDrive0 boot-sector write), T1685.005 (event-log clearing), T1505.003 (web-shell drop), T1003.001 (LSASS access) — these fire BEFORE or AT the moment of destruction and are the practical containment window for a wiper actor. IOCs are from the Unit 42 Agonizing Serpens report (2023) IOC appendix: 6 C2 IPs, 19 SHA-256 hashes (ASPXSpy web shells, NBTscan, WinEggDrop, NimScan, Mimikatz, ProcDump, Plink, Sqlextractor, pscp, and the MultiLayer/PartialWasher/BFG Agonizer wipers, GMER and Rentdrv2 driver loaders+drivers), and CVE-2018-13379 (FortiOS, exploited for initial access per SentinelLabs/MITRE). IOCs are host/campaign-specific and expire fast — TTPs and detection_signals are the durable value. No domains/emails were published in these sources; arrays left empty rather than fabricated. No verbatim YARA rule appeared in the two source reports, so yara_rules is empty (never authored from scratch).
